en: To vanish.
To go missing; to become a missing person.

disappear.ety:
From Middle English disapeeren, equivalent to dis- + appear. Displaced native Old English fordwīnan.
Displaced native Old English cwincan, whose causative persists as quench (“put out (fire)”).

ex.ja: 彼は借金を踏み倒して姿を暗ました。

ex.en: All the snow on the mountain has disappeared.
ex.ja: 山の雪がすっかり消えた。

ex.en: After 6 p.m. the employees began to disappear.
ex.ja: ６時を過ぎると従業員は帰り始めた。

en: To meet (someone) or find (something), especially unexpectedly.
To confront (someone or something) face to face.
A meeting, especially one that is unplanned or unexpected.
A hostile, often violent meeting; a confrontation, skirmish, or clash, as between combatants.

encounter.ety: From Middle English encountren, from Anglo-Norman encountrer, Old French encontrer (“to confront”), from encontre (“against, counter to”), from Late Latin incontrā (“in front of”) itself from Latin in (“in”) + contrā (“against”).

ex.en: In spring, I look forward to many encounters!
ex.ja: 春には、たくさんの出会いが待っている！

ex.en: He encountered a friend on the road.
ex.ja: 彼は道で友人と出くわした。

ex.en: Tomorrow we will encounter the enemy.
ex.ja: 明日我々は敵軍に出くわすだろう。

en: The fact of being equal.
The fact of being equal, of having the same value.

equality.ety: Borrowed from Middle French equalité (modern French égalité), from Latin aequālitās, aequālitātem. Doublet of equity. By surface analysis, equal + -ity

ex.en: He was in favor of equality for all.
ex.ja: 彼は全ての人が平等であることに賛成した。

ex.en: Women want equality of opportunity with men.
ex.ja: 女性は男性との機会の平等を要求している。

ex.en: Women have achieved equality in some areas.
ex.ja: 女性はある分野では平等を達成してきた。

note.ja: equ（等しい）+ al + ity。等しいこと →「平等」。

en: Shortened form of examine

ex.en: He got the highest grade on the exam.
ex.ja: 彼は試験で最高点をとった。

ex.en: He made every effort to pass the exam.
ex.ja: 彼は試験に合格しようとあらゆる努力をした。

ex.en: She was happy that she passed the exam.
ex.ja: 彼女は試験に合格してうれしかった。

en: The act of examining.
Particularly, an inspection by a medical professional to establish the extent and nature of any sickness or injury.

examination.ety: From Middle English examinacioun, from Old French examinacion, from Latin exāminātiō. Morphologically examine + -ation.

ex.en: In addition to that, he failed the examination.
ex.ja: そのことに加えて、彼は試験に失敗した。

ex.en: My brother is taking the entrance examination today.
ex.ja: 兄は今日入学試験を受けている。

ex.en: Are you going to take the entrance examination?
ex.ja: 入学試験を受けるつもりですか。

en: An act of joining together into a single political entity.
An array of nations or states that are unified under one central authority.
Of an architectural style popular around the time of federation.

federation.ety: Borrowed from French fédération, from Late Latin foederatio, from Latin foederare; equivalent to federate + -ion.

note.ja: ラテン語 foedus（同盟・契約）から。信頼で結ばれた連合 →「連邦・連盟」。fid（信頼）と同じ祖先 *bʰeydʰ-。

en: Related to the treasury of a country, company, region or city, particularly to government spending and revenue.
Pertaining to finance and money in general; financial.
A public official in certain countries having control of public revenue.
Procurator fiscal, a public prosecutor.

fiscal.ety: From Middle French fiscal, from Latin fiscus (“treasury”) – see fiscus and fisc.

ex.en: The scholar is an authority on fiscal policy.
ex.ja: その学者は財政政策の権威である。

ex.en: Developing countries suffer from difficulties of fiscal problems.
ex.ja: 発展途上国は財政問題で諸々の困難に苦しんでいる。

ex.en: They labored over the budget for the fiscal year 1997.
ex.ja: 彼らは苦労して１９９７会計年度の予算を作成した。

en: Someone who guards, watches over, or protects.
A person legally responsible for a minor (in loco parentis).

guardian.ety: From Middle English gardein, garden, (also wardein, > Modern English warden), from Old French guardein, from the verb guarder, of Germanic origin. Compare French gardien. Doublet of warden. By surface analysis, guard + -ian.

ex.en: I regard myself as your guardian.
ex.ja: 私はきみの保護者のつもりだ。

ex.en: Minors must have a parent or guardian sign the form.
ex.ja: 未成年の方は、保護者のサインをもらってください。

ex.en: John acts like Helen's guardian.
ex.ja: ジョンはヘレンの保護者のようにふるまっている。

en: One who loves and cares for another person in a romantic way; a sweetheart, love, soulmate, boyfriend, girlfriend, or spouse.
A sexual partner, especially one with whom someone is having an affair.

lover.ety: From Middle English lovere, luffer, lufere, equivalent to love + -er.

ex.en: We're lovers so we hold hands at least, right?
ex.ja: 俺達、恋人同士なんだから手ぐらいつなぐよね。

ex.en: What's the difference between a friend and a lover?
ex.ja: 友達と恋人の違いって何なんだろう。

ex.en: He's what society calls a real lover of music.
ex.ja: 彼は世間でいう音楽の真の愛好者だ。

en: Used or accepted broadly rather than by small portions of population, market, scientific community, etc.
The principal current in a flow, such as a river or flow of air
That which is common; the norm.
To popularize, to normalize, to render mainstream.
To become mainstream.

mainstream.ety: From main + stream. Cognate with Icelandic meginstraumur (“a main current, mainstream”).

ex.ja: ユダヤ正統派の主流から外れた部分においては、黙示録はある種の運動に対して、より成功を収めたのである。

en: The details of the food to be served at a banquet; a bill of fare.
A list containing the food and beverages served at a restaurant, café, or bar. Menus may be printed on paper sheets provided to customers…

menu.ety: Borrowed from French menu. Doublet of menudo and minute.

ex.ja: これはメニューに書かれてあった内容とちがっています。

ex.en: Do you have any questions about the menu?
ex.ja: 料理について何か質問がありますか。

ex.en: Do you have a menu in English?
ex.ja: 英語のメニューはありますか？

en: Having the same relationship, each to each other.
Collective, done or held in common.
A mutual fund.
A mutual organization.

mutual.ety: Borrowed from Middle French mutuel, from Latin mūtuus. Displaced native Old English ġemǣne.

ex.ja: やめろよ。あいつは俺たちの友達だろ。

ex.en: It's necessary that we come to a mutual understanding.
ex.ja: 我々の相互理解が必要である。

ex.en: They gave mutual help to each other.
ex.ja: 彼らは相互に助け合った。

note.ja: ラテン語 mutuus（交換された）から。mut（変える・交換する）。互いに交わし合う →「相互の・共通の」。

en: A crime or sin.
An affront, injury, or insult.

offense.ety: From Middle English offence, from Old French offense, from Latin offensa (“a striking against; displeasure; injury”).

ex.en: He committed an offense against our laws.
ex.ja: 彼は我が国の法律に違反した。

ex.en: He is quick to take offense.
ex.ja: 彼は直に腹を立てる。

ex.en: I'm sorry, I meant no offence.
ex.ja: すいません、悪気はなかったんです。

en: Relating to the mouth.
Done or taken by the mouth.
A spoken test or examination, particularly in a language class.
A physical examination of the mouth.

ex.ja: 彼女は上司に口頭で報告をした。

ex.ja: 彼が署名した契約書がなければ、彼の口頭での同意は何の意味もないだろう。

ex.en: She had an oral examination in English.
ex.ja: 彼女は英語の口頭試験を受けた。

en: Of fear, fright, etc: overwhelming or sudden.
Pertaining to or resulting from overwhelming fear or fright.
Overwhelming fear or fright, often affecting groups of people or animals; (countable) an instance of this; a fright, a scare.
A rapid reduction in asset prices due to broad efforts to raise cash in anticipation of such prices continuing to decline.
To cause (someone) to feel panic (“overwhelming fear or fright”); also, to frighten (someone) into acting hastily.
To cause (a computer system) to crash.

panic.ety:
The adjective is borrowed from Middle French panique, a word itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πανικός (panikós, “pertaining to Pan”); Pan, the Greek god of fields and woods, was believed to be the source of mysterious sounds that caused contagious, groundless fear in herds and crowds, or in people in lonely spots.
Adjective sense 3 (“pertaining to or resulting from overpowering fear or fright”) is partly an attributive use of the noun.
The noun is derived from the adjective, while the verb is derived from the noun. Verb sense 1.3 (“to highly amuse, entertain, or impress (an audience watching

ex.en: The fire caused a panic in the theater.
ex.ja: 火事で劇場の中は大混乱になった。

ex.en: There's no need to panic. There's plenty of time.
ex.ja: そんなにあわてることはないよ。時間はたっぷりあるんだから。

ex.en: There's no reason to panic. Just handle it quickly.
ex.ja: オタオタしてないで、はやくその問題を解決しなさい！

en: To follow urgently, originally with intent to capture or harm; to chase.
To follow, travel down (a particular way, course of action etc.).

pursue.ety: From Middle English pursuen, from Anglo-Norman pursure, poursuire etc., from Latin prōsequor (though influenced by persequor). Doublet of prosecute.

ex.ja: 彼女はインテリア・デザインの仕事をしていきたいと考えている。

ex.en: Students often pursue their teacher with questions.
ex.ja: 学生はしばしば先生を質問攻めにする。

ex.en: I plan to pursue a career in international finance.
ex.ja: 国際金融で仕事を続けるつもりです。

en: A person seeking refuge (as for shelter or protection), especially in a foreign country, out of fear or prospect of political, religious …
To convey (slaves) away from the advance of the federal forces.

refugee.ety: From French réfugié, past participle of réfugier (“to take refuge, to seek refuge”), from Old French refuge (“hiding place”) from Latin refugium (“a place of refuge, place to flee back to”), originally describing French Huguenots fleeing religious persecution after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685. Noun sense 1 was "one seeking asylum" until 1914, when it evolved to mean more generally "one fleeing home" (first applied in this sense to civilians in Flanders heading west to escape fighting in World War I). By surface analysis, refuge + -ee. Displaced native Old English flīema.

ex.en: The refugees are well set up with food.
ex.ja: 難民たちは食料を十分に供給されている。

ex.en: They established a Japanese language class for the refugees.
ex.ja: 彼らは難民たちのために日本語の授業を設立した。

ex.en: Refugees in Africa are seeking help.
ex.ja: アフリカの難民が救いを求めている。

en: To divide or separate the parts of (especially something flimsy, such as paper or fabric), by cutting or tearing; to tear off or out by v…
To tear apart; to rapidly become two parts.
A tear (in paper, etc.).
A rip current: a strong outflow of surface water, away from the shore, that returns water from incoming waves.

rip.ety:
From Middle English rippen, from earlier ryppen (“to pluck”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rupjaną and/or *ruppōną, intensive of *raupijaną, causative of Proto-Indo-European *Hrewp- (“to break”). Possible doublet of rub.
Cognate with West Frisian rippe, ripje, roppe, ropje (“to rip”), Dutch dialectal rippen, Low German ruppen, German Low German röpen, German rupfen, also Old English rīpan, rīepan (“to plunder”) (whence English reap), West Frisian rippe (“to rip, tear”), German raufen (“to rip”); perhaps also, less likely, Albanian rrabe (“maquis”) and Latin rubus (“bramble”). More at reave,

ex.en: He ripped up all her letters and photos.
ex.ja: 彼は彼女の手紙と写真をすべて切り裂いた。

ex.ja: そんなに引っ張らないで、服が破れるでしょ！

ex.ja: トムは時々、彼のお客をだましてお金をまきあげる。

To risk or offer.

Perfectly.

pat.ety: From Middle English pat (“a blow, stroke”), alteration (with loss of medial l) of *plat (> Scots plat (“a blow, buffet”)), from Old English plætt (“a sounding blow, a smack”), from Proto-West Germanic *platt (“a smack, slap, blow”), from Proto-Germanic *plat- (“to strike, beat”), from Proto-Indo-European *blod-, *bled- (“to strike, beat”). spy.ety:
From Middle English spien, aphetic variant of earlier espien (“to espy”), from Old French espier (“to spy”), from Frankish *spehōn (“to spy”), from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”). Akin to German spähen (“to spy”), Dutch spieden (“to spy”).
The noun displaced native Old English sċēawere (literally “watcher”), which was also the word for "mirror." In this sense, the verb displaced Old English sċēawian, which was also the word for "to watch" and became the Modern English word show.

ex.ja: その新しいホテルではお客さんに意見を求めた。

note.ja: sug（下から）+ gest（運ぶ）+ ion。下からそっと持ち出すこと →「提案・示唆」。
